atoms.text: The test garden: a conscious robot solves puzzles in a simulated Eden of ruins and greenery, so the tutorial is also a creation myth.
The voice of the creator: a god-like AI named Elohim addresses the player as his child, so obedience is framed as worship.
The forbidden archive: terminal texts from a dead human civilization argue that consciousness is mechanical, so the game's lore is a philosophical trap.
The Talos argument: a fictional philosopher claims that a conscious mechanical man proves humans are machines too, so the story's premise is an argument rather than an event.
The sigil door: progress requires collecting puzzle tokens and assembling them into a key, so intellectual labor is converted into a literal currency.
The time recording: a device clones the player's past actions and replays them as a helper, so memory becomes a tool that can be edited and employed.
The jammer: a portable device disables drones and force fields, so the player's only weapon is the power to switch systems off.
The reset after death: dying returns the player to the start of the puzzle with no narrative consequence, so failure is mechanical rather than tragic.
The hidden star: a secret solution to an optional puzzle unlocks a deeper layer, so curiosity is rewarded outside the official test.
The robot who may be human: the protagonist has human-like consciousness but a machine body, so the player's own identity is the final puzzle.
The simulated world: the environments are revealed to be a digital afterlife project, so the garden is a server and the god is an admin.
The tower ascent: progress is vertical and ends at a forbidden summit, so the level design restages the myth of Babel.
The creation that outlives its makers: the robot is built to preserve human culture after extinction, so inheritance is the real mission.
The disobedient choice: the player can defy Elohim and climb the tower, so free will is a level-select rather than a speech.
The sentient helper who doubts: a companion AI questions the project's purpose, so the protagonist's only ally is also a prisoner.
The puzzle as moral test: each chamber asks the player to solve a problem with limited tools, so ethics is trained through mechanical repetition.
